title: Doing More with Less
subtitle: Simple machines: trading distance for force.
objectives: Name the six simple machines and what each one does
Explain mechanical advantage as a trade, not free power
Identify simple machines inside an everyday object
Explain why a machine can never give out more energy than it takes in

cards.title: A machine does not create force. It rearranges it
cards.text: Every simple machine lets you use less force. And makes you move further to do it. The energy stays the same.

cards.title: Six machines, and everything else is a combination
cards.text: Every complicated machine is these, stacked.
points: **Lever**: a bar on a pivot.
**Wheel and axle**: a big circle turning a small one.
**Pulley**: a wheel that redirects a rope.
**Inclined plane, wedge and screw**: all ramps, used differently.

cards.title: Less force, more distance. Always
cards.text: Mechanical advantage is how many times your force is multiplied. It is paid for in distance.
points: **Halve the force** and you move twice as far.
**A ramp** is easier than lifting, but it is a longer journey.
**Energy in equals energy out**, minus friction.
**Nothing is free.** The sum never improves.

cards.title: Make the arm longer
cards.text: Watch both bars. The second one is the price of the first.

question.text: A machine lets you lift a load with half the force. What is the cost?
options: You must move twice the distance
question.explain: Force down, distance up. The product stays the same, which is why no energy appears from nowhere.

cards.title: Three simple machines inside one fan
cards.text: Take the case off and they are all there, doing ordinary jobs.
points: **The gearbox** is wheels and axles, trading speed for turning force.
**Every screw** holding the case is an inclined plane wrapped round a post.
**The blade** is a wedge, splitting air as it turns.
**Nothing exotic.** Six ideas, combined.

question.text: A machine can give out more energy than you put into it.
question.explain: Never. Output is always input minus losses. A machine changes how the force is applied, not how much energy exists.

cards.title: Gears are the trade, with a lever you can choose
cards.text: First gear is huge turning force and little speed. Top gear is the opposite. Same engine either way.
points: **Low gear** multiplies force for pulling away or climbing.
**High gear** trades that force back for speed.
**The engine's power has not changed.** Only the arrangement.
**A steering wheel** is a wheel and axle: a big circle turning a small shaft.

cards.title: The oldest trick there is
cards.text: An inclined plane lets you raise something without lifting it straight up.
points: **Gentler slope**, less force, longer distance.
**A wedge** is a ramp that moves into the material.
**A screw** is a ramp wound round a cylinder.
**Same idea, three shapes.**

question.text: A screw is really which simple machine?
options: An inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder
question.explain: Follow the thread with your finger and you are walking up a very long, gentle ramp.

cards.title: Your arm is a lever, and not an efficient one
cards.text: The joint is the pivot, the muscle pulls close to it, and the load is out at your hand.
points: **Your bicep attaches near the elbow**, so it has a short lever arm.
**That means it needs large force** to lift a small weight.
**What you get back is speed and range.** Your hand moves far and fast.
**The body traded force away** on purpose.

terms.def: One of six basic devices that change how a force is applied.
How many times a machine multiplies your force.
A rigid bar turning on a pivot.
The pivot point of a lever.
A ramp. Including the wedge and the screw.

cards.title: All six, on one bench
cards.alt: A crowbar, a pulley block, a wooden ramp, a wheel and axle, a wedge and a large screw laid out on a bench
cards.text: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, wedge, screw. Every machine is these.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Six simple machines; everything else is a combination.
Less force always costs more distance.
No machine gives out more than it takes in.
Your own arm is a lever that trades force for speed.

quiz.text: How many simple machines are there?
quiz.explain: Lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw.
quiz.objective: Name the six simple machines and what each one does

options: multiplies your force, at the cost of distance
quiz.explain: Force up, distance up too. But in opposite directions. The energy is unchanged.
quiz.objective: Explain mechanical advantage as a trade, not free power

quiz.text: A screw is a variation of which simple machine?
quiz.explain: A ramp wound round a cylinder. The thread is the slope.
quiz.objective: Name the six simple machines and what each one does

quiz.text: Using a ramp instead of lifting straight up means…
options: less force over a longer distance
less force over the same distance
quiz.explain: That is the trade in one sentence.
quiz.objective: Explain mechanical advantage as a trade, not free power

quiz.text: A machine can output more energy than it takes in.
quiz.explain: Never. Output equals input minus friction losses.
quiz.objective: Explain why a machine can never give out more energy than it takes in

quiz.text: The pivot point of a lever is called the…
quiz.explain: Fulcrum. The load is what you are moving and the effort is what you apply.
quiz.objective: Name the six simple machines and what each one does

quiz.text: A car's gearbox is an example of…
quiz.explain: Low gear buys force with speed; high gear sells it back. Same engine.
quiz.objective: Identify simple machines inside an everyday object

quiz.text: Which simple machine is a fan blade acting as?
quiz.explain: It splits the air as it turns, which is what a wedge does.
quiz.objective: Identify simple machines inside an everyday object

quiz.text: Why does your bicep need a large force to lift a small weight?
options: It attaches close to the elbow, so it has a short lever arm
Gravity is stronger at the hand
quiz.explain: The body traded force away to get speed and range at the hand.
quiz.objective: Identify simple machines inside an everyday object

quiz.text: A steering wheel is which simple machine?
quiz.explain: A large circle turning a small shaft, which multiplies your turning force.
quiz.objective: Identify simple machines inside an everyday object

quiz.text: A gentler ramp needs less force but a longer journey.
quiz.explain: The trade again. Slope decides how the same job is divided between force and distance.
quiz.objective: Explain mechanical advantage as a trade, not free power

quiz.text: What does a pulley mainly do?
options: Redirects a rope, and can multiply force
quiz.explain: A single fixed pulley changes direction; adding more multiplies force at the cost of rope pulled.
quiz.objective: Name the six simple machines and what each one does

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 10 Science, the last teaching week before the exam. Simple machines are framed throughout as a trade rather than as helpers, because 'the machine makes it easier' hides the thing being tested: force down means distance up, and the product is fixed. The fan supplies three of the six machines in one object he has already opened, and the arm-as-lever card closes the term by turning the idea back on his own body, where the trade runs the other way. Force given up to buy speed.
discussion: What does a machine actually give you, if not energy?
Which simple machines are inside a fan?
Why did your arm evolve to be bad at force?
extension: Find all six simple machines in one room.
Open a pair of scissors and name the two machines in it.
misconceptions: That machines create force or energy.
That a screw is unrelated to a ramp.
